info.bio:
The Weavers were an American folk music quartet based in the Greenwich Village area of New York City. 
The Weavers were formed in November 1948 by Ronnie Gilbert, Pete Seeger, Lee Hays and Fred Hellerman.
They sang traditional folk songs from around the world, as well as blues, gospel music, children's songs, labor songs, and American ballads, and sold millions of records at the height of their popularity. Their hard-driving string-band style inspired the commercial "folk boom" that followed them in the 1950s and 1960s

scenes.name: Country blues
scenes.author: Ted Gioia
scenes.desc: La cara liberadora y dionisíaca del ritmo africano: un medio para expresar dolor, opresión y deseo sin autocompasión, con un efecto catártico comparable al de la tragedia. Lo conocemos por grabaciones a partir de los años veinte. Forma de doce compases (tónica, dominante, subdominante) con blue notes que oscilan entre tercera mayor y menor, y estrofa AAB; pero los cantantes del campo alargan o acortan los compases a su antojo porque cantan solos con su guitarra. Charlie Patton, más antiguo y ligado a la plantación, dialoga con su guitarra; Blind Lemon Jefferson canta agudo y fino en Texas; Leadbelly, descubierto en una cárcel por los Lomax, acaba en Nueva York; Robert Johnson, tardío y casi desconocido en vida, se convierte en el paradigma del Delta. Gioia duda del origen en los griots africanos: el blues es un tipo de canción nuevo, nacido en el Sur.

podcast.title: Blacklisting During McCarthy Era
podcast.body: Both Pete Seeger and Lee Hayes were named as past Communist Party members and called before the House on American Activities Committee to testify. As a result, The Weavers were blacklisted from radio and TV, causing "Wimoweh" to drop off the chart and their recording catalogue to be deleted. "Wimmer Way went to number 6 on the charts, but then sent it to McCarthy Stepton."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 92: "The Lion Sleeps Tonight" by the Tokens

podcast.title: Commercial Success
podcast.body: The Weavers achieved far more commercial success than The Almanac Singers, recording hit versions of songs like "Good Night Irene" and "Wimoweh." "The weavers immediately had far more commercial success than the Almanac singers ever had, and recorded such hits as their version of Lead Belly's Good Night Irene, with orchestration by Gordon Jenkins."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 92: "The Lion Sleeps Tonight" by the Tokens

podcast.title: Continuation of The Almanac Singers
podcast.body: The Weavers were formed by Pete Seeger and Lee Hayes more or less as a continuation of The Almanac Singers, but with a less explicitly political agenda. They performed songs by Woody Guthrie and Lead Belly, and their own material, without being tied to a specific ideological line. "But the core of the group had been Seeger and Lee Hayes, and those two had eventually formed another group, more or less as a continuation of the Almanac singers, but with a less explicitly political agenda."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Dylan's Acknowledgment of Influence
podcast.body: Bob Dylan would sometimes introduce his own song "Let Me Die In My Footsteps," a successful early composition about nuclear war, as a Weavers' song. "His first truly successful song, a song about nuclear war, let me die in my footsteps. He would introduce as a weaver's song."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 97: "Song to Woody" by Bob Dylan

podcast.title: Eric Darling Replaces Seeger
podcast.body: Following Pete Seeger's departure, he suggested Eric Darling from the folk group The Tarriers as his replacement. Darling, an "Ironman fan and a Libertarian," presumably held different views on advertising than Seeger. "At his suggestion, he was replaced by Eric Darling from another folk group that Tarias."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 92: "The Lion Sleeps Tonight" by the Tokens

podcast.title: Influence on John Denver
podcast.body: The folk music of The Weavers likely influenced a young Henry John Deutschendorf Jr. (John Denver) as he learned to play his first guitar. "This is the Weavers, which we're playing because young Henry John Doichendorf Jr. was likely trying to play it on his first guitar."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
srcs.episode: Country Roads and Summer Nights Edition Part 1

podcast.title: Pete Seeger's Departure Over Tobacco Commercial
podcast.body: After reuniting for a hit live album, Pete Seeger permanently left the group a couple of years later when they did a commercial for tobacco. While the group saw it as an opportunity for exposure due to being blacklisted, Seeger disapproved of tobacco and advertising. He did appear in the commercial due to a prior commitment, not wanting to break his word. "Seeger left the group permanently a couple of years after that, when they did a commercial for tobacco."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 92: "The Lion Sleeps Tonight" by the Tokens

podcast.title: Spawned from Armanac House
podcast.body: The Weavers emerged from the environment of left-wing intellectuals and folk singers centered in Armanac House in Greenwich Village, alongside The Armanac Singers. "It was this environment, centered in Armanac House in Greenwich Village, that spawned the Armanac singers and later the weavers"

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 97: "Song to Woody" by Bob Dylan

concerts.title: Carnegie Hall (1955)
concerts.body: The group reunited after being blacklisted from radio and TV and performed a concert at Carnegie Hall in 1955, which resulted in a hit live album that included their version of "Wimoweh." "The groups split up, though they did get back together again a few years later, and managed to have a hit live album of a concert they performed at Carnegie Hall in 1955, which also included Wimmer Way."
